title: Provincial & Territorial R&D Tax Credits - SR&ED Glossary
description: Explore Provincial/Territorial R&D Tax Credits across Canada and how they stack with federal SR&ED in our tax glossary.
summary: Provincial and territorial R&D tax credits give Canadian businesses that claim federal SR&ED a second layer of support: nine provinces and Yukon offer them, while Prince Edward Island, the Northwest Territories and Nunavut do not. Rates range from Ontario's 3.5% non-refundable credit to Quebec's 30% refundable CRIC, and each credit reduces federal qualified expenditures as government assistance.

body.text: Provincial and territorial R&D tax credits give Canadian businesses that claim federal SR&ED a second layer of support: nine provinces and Yukon offer them, while Prince Edward Island, the Northwest Territories and Nunavut do not. Rates range from Ontario's 3.5% non-refundable credit to Quebec's 30% refundable CRIC, and each credit reduces federal qualified expenditures as government assistance.

Canada's flagship R&D fiscal mechanism—the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program, which supports more than 24,160 businesses annually, with small businesses representing 65% of all claims submitted in the 2025–2026 fiscal year—has undergone its most significant legislative and administrative modernization in over a decade following the enactment of Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Effective for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, Bill C-15 doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% federal Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3 million to $6 million (increasing the maximum annual refundable federal cash benefit from $1.05 million to $2.1 million), expanded the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range for Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, and extended eligibility for the 35% enhanced refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) based on a three-year average gross revenue phase-out test. Furthermore, for property acquired and lease costs first becoming payable on or after December 16, 2024, Parliament restored the eligibility of SR&ED capital expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and equipment lease costs, which had been repealed since January 1, 2014.

Simultaneously, federal administrative procedures and provincial R&D regimes have shifted substantially. On April 1, 2026, the CRA launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval process (utilizing Form T1322 through My Business Account), enabling eligible businesses with gross business income under $25 million to obtain an upfront technical eligibility determination within eight weeks prior to incurring project costs. At the provincial level, Quebec abolished six legacy R&D tax credit measures for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, consolidating them into the fully refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC / crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation), which provides a 30% credit on the first $1 million of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures above an exclusion threshold and 20% on excess spending. Similarly, the March 18, 2026 Saskatchewan Budget doubled the refundable 10% R&D tax credit expenditure limit for CCPCs from $1 million to $2 million and restored provincial capital expenditure eligibility expected to take effect for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024.
1. Statutory and Legislative Architecture of the SR&ED Program
1.1 Dual-Pillar Structure Under the Income Tax Act

Canada's federal SR&ED tax incentive program operates through a dual-pillar statutory framework embedded within the Income Tax Act (ITA) and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations. Unlike single-tier tax credit regimes in other jurisdictions, calculating a Canadian SR&ED claim requires executing two interrelated but legally distinct computations. The first calculation determines the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures under Section 37 of the ITA, while the second determines qualified SR&ED expenditures for the Investment Tax Credit (ITC) under Section 127 and Section 127.1 of the ITA.

Under the first pillar, subsection 37(1) of the ITA governs the calculation of a taxpayer's cumulative pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures. A taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada may deduct in computing business income for a taxation year an amount not exceeding the balance of their cumulative SR&ED expenditure pool at the end of that year. Any unclaimed balance in the Section 37 pool does not expire and may be carried forward indefinitely to offset business income in future taxation years, subject to loss restriction event rules under paragraph 37(1)(h) and subsection 37(6.1) if an acquisition of control occurs.

Under the second pillar, Section 127 of the ITA establishes the calculation of "qualified expenditures" and the resulting SR&ED Investment Tax Credit, which directly offsets federal Part I tax otherwise payable under subsection 127(5). Section 127.1 of the ITA governs the "refundable investment tax credit" rules, authorizing the Minister of National Revenue to issue direct cash refunds for unused ITCs to qualifying CCPCs, non-qualifying CCPCs (on current expenditures within their expenditure limit), ECPCs, individuals, and certain trusts.

Because an expenditure can be deductible under Section 37 without generating an equivalent qualified expenditure under Section 127—and conversely, notional or capital-based additions such as the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) or Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) inclusions generate ITCs under Section 127 without ever entering the Section 37 deduction pool—taxpayers and auditors must never treat "allowable SR&ED expenditures" and "qualified SR&ED expenditures" as interchangeable terms. Furthermore, under paragraph 37(1)(e) of the ITA, any federal SR&ED ITC deducted against Part I tax or refunded in cash in a given taxation year must be deducted from the Section 37 expenditure pool in the immediately following taxation year (reported on Line 435 of Form T661), thereby preventing a double benefit on the same dollar of expenditure and effectively taxing the prior year's credit. If the prior-year ITC reduction exceeds the available Section 37 pool balance, the excess negative balance must be included in the taxpayer's business income under paragraph 12(1)(v), and any such inclusion is subsequently accounted for in the pool under paragraph 37(1)(c.1).
1.2 Core Statutory Citations and Regulatory Provisions

The legal validity of any Canadian SR&ED claim rests on strict compliance with specific sections of the Income Tax Act and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations. Subsection 248(1) of the ITA contains the exhaustive statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" (paragraphs (a) through (k)), alongside the statutory definitions of "salary or wages" and "specified employee" (which captures shareholder-employees and employees not dealing at arm's length with the claimant).

Section 37 of the ITA governs the expenditure pool. Paragraph 37(1)(a) provides for the inclusion of current expenditures on SR&ED carried on in Canada directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer (subparagraphs (i) and (i.01)) and eligible third-party payments to corporations, approved associations, universities, colleges, research institutes, and paragraph 149(1)(j) non-profit SR&ED corporations (subparagraphs (i.1), (ii), and (iii)). Restored paragraph 37(1)(b) provides for the inclusion of capital expenditures made after December 15, 2024, on depreciable property for SR&ED in Canada. Related provisions within Section 37 govern related-corporation business linkages (subsection 37(1.1)), available-for-use timing for capital property (subsection 37(1.2)), work within Canada's Exclusive Economic Zone, airspace, seabed, or subsoil (subsection 37(1.3)), permissible foreign salary or wages capped at 10% of Canadian SR&ED salaries (subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5)), current expenditures for SR&ED outside Canada (subsection 37(2)), ministerial consultation with the Department of Industry, the National Research Council of Canada, or the Defence Research Board (subsection 37(3)), the prohibition on deducting costs to acquire rights in or arising out of SR&ED (subsection 37(4)), deemed capital cost allowance (CCA) treatment for SR&ED capital expenditures (subsection 37(6)), loss restriction events (subsection 37(6.1)), building exclusions (paragraph 37(8)(e)), specified employee bonus exclusions and the 5× Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) salary cap (subsections 37(9) to 37(9.5)), the mandatory 12-month post-filing-due-date reporting deadline (subsections 37(11), 37(11.1), and 37(12)), and non-arm's length linked work (subsection 37(13)). Significantly, Bill C-15 (S.C. 2026, c. 3, s. 5) repealed former subsections 37(14) and 37(15)—which previously enforced the post-2013 capital "look-through rule" reducing contract and third-party payments by a performer's capital or lease costs—effective for property acquired and lease costs first becoming payable on or after December 16, 2024.

Sections 127 and 127.1 of the ITA govern the Investment Tax Credit. Subsection 127(5) authorizes the deduction of ITCs from Part I tax otherwise payable, while subsections 127(8) to 127(8.4) govern partnership ITC allocations and renunciations. Subsection 127(9) houses the foundational definitions of "investment tax credit", "qualified expenditure", "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool", "contract payment", "government assistance", "non-government assistance", "excluded loan", "first term shared-use-equipment", "second term shared-use-equipment", "taxable supplier", "eligible Canadian public corporation", "eligible subsidiary", and "specified percentage". Subsections 127(10.1) to 127(10.64) establish the enhanced 35% ITC and the $6 million expenditure limit and phase-out formulas for CCPCs and ECPCs. Subsection 127(11.5) and subsection 127(11.6) govern adjustments to qualified expenditures and non-arm's length cost caps; subsection 127(13) governs non-arm's length qualified expenditure transfers; subsections 127(18) to 127(20) mandate reductions for government assistance, non-government assistance, and contract payments; subsection 127(26) excludes unpaid non-wage current expenditures after 180 days; and subsections 127(27) to 127(36) enforce the 20-year ITC recapture regime. Section 127.1 defines "qualifying corporation", "excluded corporation", "qualifying income limit", and "refundable investment tax credit", establishing the 100% and 40% cash refundability mechanisms under subsections 127.1(1), 127.1(2), and 127.1(2.01).

Finally, Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (Sections 2900 to 2903) provides the detailed regulatory mechanics. Section 2900 defines traditional method directly attributable overhead and facility inclusions (subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3)), the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) formula (subsection 2900(4)), the overall PPA cap (subsections 2900(5) and 2900(6)), the specified employee proxy salary base limits (subsections 2900(7), 2900(8), and 2900(9)), and Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) exclusions (subsection 2900(11)). Section 2901 prescribes eligible foreign universities; Section 2902 defines prescribed current and capital expenditures excluded from qualified expenditures; and Section 2903 governs prescribed special-purpose buildings.
1.3 Legislative Evolution: From the 2024 Fall Economic Statement to Bill C-15 (2026)

A critical verification point for corporate tax planners and auditors is the multi-stage legislative evolution between late 2024 and March 2026. In the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES 2024), the Department of Finance initially proposed raising the enhanced 35% ITC expenditure limit from $3 million to $4.5 million, expanding the taxable capital phase-out range to $15 million–$75 million, extending the enhanced credit to ECPCs, and restoring capital expenditure eligibility effective December 16, 2024. Subsequently, in Federal Budget 2025, the government confirmed all FES 2024 measures and further increased the proposed enhanced expenditure limit from $4.5 million to $6 million.

On March 26, 2026, Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1) received Royal Assent, codifying the $6 million expenditure limit and all accompanying modernization reforms into law. Additionally, earlier legislation under Bill C-69 (which received Royal Assent on June 20, 2024) amended subsection 127(9) of the ITA retroactively to January 1, 2020, to introduce the concept of an "excluded loan", ensuring that bona fide government loans with reasonable repayment terms made after December 31, 2019, do not erode a claimant's SR&ED expenditure pool or qualified expenditures as government assistance.

body.text: 2. Scientific and Technological Eligibility Framework
2.1 The Statutory Definition Under Subsection 248(1)

Since 1996, the legal definition of SR&ED has been codified in subsection 248(1) of the ITA. It defines "scientific research and experimental development" as a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis and that falls into one of four eligible categories across paragraphs (a) through (d).

Paragraph (a) covers basic research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Basic research expands the fundamental scientific knowledge base and is most commonly conducted in laboratory settings by universities, research institutes, and emerging biotechnology or nanotechnology enterprises, with findings frequently published in scientific journals. An example of basic research is studying a newly discovered virus solely to understand its molecular structure and replication characteristics.

Paragraph (b) covers applied research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Following the viral example above, conducting systematic laboratory experiments to develop a vaccine against that newly discovered virus by exploiting its specific molecular characteristics constitutes applied research.

Paragraph (c) covers experimental development, defined as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Experimental development is the primary category claimed by industrial, manufacturing, and software enterprises in Canada (such as scaling up and optimizing bioprocess parameters to enable rapid, large-scale commercial manufacturing of the vaccine when existing process models fail). Crucially, commercial failure or the inability to achieve a desired performance target does not disqualify a project; the technological advancement resides in the new technological knowledge or conceptual understanding gained through the work (such as proving why a specific material formulation or software architecture fails under defined constraints), rather than in producing a commercially successful product.

Paragraph (d) covers support work, defined as work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, where the work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of work described in paragraph (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. Support work is never eligible on a standalone basis; it must correspond strictly in amount, size, extent, and duration to the needs of the core basic research, applied research, or experimental development.
2.2 The "Why" and "How" Requirements vs. the Five-Question Framework

In August 2021, the CRA replaced its archived Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy with the current Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives. The 2021 guidelines synthesize the statutory test into two foundational requirements—the "Why" and the "How"—which are derived from the unchanged statutory definition in subsection 248(1) and mirror the common-law five-question framework articulated by Chief Justice Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839 (TCC).
The "Why" Requirement: Scientific or Technological Uncertainty and Advancement

Under the "Why" requirement, the work must be conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement. The CRA guidelines emphasize that eligible work must seek the generation or discovery of conceptual knowledge (such as explanatory theories or predictive models) rather than merely factual knowledge (such as routine measurements or observations). New knowledge is required only when a scientific or technological uncertainty exists—meaning that whether a given objective can be achieved, or how to achieve it, cannot be known or determined on the basis of generally available scientific or technological knowledge or experience (standard practice or competent routine engineering).

To assist claimants and Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) in recognizing when available technological knowledge is insufficient, the CRA guidelines identify eight specific problem characteristics that indicate technological uncertainty: existing design methods are not applicable; requirements or specifications do not conform to existing standards; there are too many interacting variables or unknowns; operating parameters or conditions fall outside the normal operating range; the nature of the problem is dynamically evolving; required data is not readily available; interlocking constraints prevent standard resolution; or stringent economic considerations and cost targets impose a genuine technological uncertainty. Conversely, circumventing a technical uncertainty through a known workaround, or acquiring existing knowledge via staff training, on-the-job learning, hiring expert employees or consultants to apply what they already know, or purchasing proprietary knowledge does not satisfy the "Why" requirement.
The "How" Requirement: Systematic Investigation or Search

Under the "How" requirement, the work must be executed via a disciplined, systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. Under both CRA administrative policy and binding Federal Court of Appeal jurisprudence, a systematic investigation requires four sequential steps:

items: Defining a Problem and Formulating a Hypothesis: Generating a testable idea consistent with known facts—expressed as a proposed solution, method, or architectural approach—that serves as a starting point for further investigation toward resolving the scientific or technological uncertainty.

Planning and Testing the Hypothesis by Experiment or Analysis: Methodically testing the idea or hypothesis through controlled experiments or mathematical/engineering analysis, allowing the hypothesis to evolve and change iteratively as test results are observed.
Developing Logical Conclusions: Analyzing the results or findings of the experiments or analyses to formulate logical conclusions regarding the hypothesis.
Keeping Contemporaneous Evidence: Maintaining dated records and evidence of the hypotheses tested and the results obtained as the work progresses.

body.text: These two requirements map directly onto the five-question framework used in CRA eligibility reviews and Tax Court litigation: (1) Was there a scientific or technological uncertainty? (2) Did the effort involve formulating hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty? (3) Was the overall approach adopted consistent with a systematic investigation or search, including formulating and testing the hypotheses by means of experiment or analysis? (4) Was the overall approach undertaken for the purpose of achieving a scientific or technological advancement? and (5) Was a record of the hypotheses tested and the results kept as the work progressed?
2.3 Statutorily Excluded Activities (Paragraphs (e) to (k))

Even where a broader business project involves innovation, paragraphs (e) through (k) of the definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) of the ITA explicitly exclude seven specific lettered categories of work from qualifying as SR&ED:

items: Paragraph (e): Market research or sales promotion;
Paragraph (f): Quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes;
Paragraph (g): Research in the social sciences or the humanities;
Paragraph (h): Prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas;
Paragraph (i): The commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process;
Paragraph (j): Style changes; and
Paragraph (k): Routine data collection.

body.text: When auditing claims that involve both eligible support work under paragraph (d) and excluded work under paragraphs (e) through (k) (such as distinguishing eligible "data collection" from excluded "routine data collection", or eligible "testing" from excluded "routine testing"), the CRA evaluates purpose. If data collection or testing is carried out specifically and exclusively to support basic research, applied research, or experimental development, it qualifies as eligible support work under paragraph (d); if it is performed for normal commercial operations, quality control, or mineral prospecting, it must be segregated and excluded from the claim.
3. Qualifying Expenditures and Calculation Methodologies
3.1 Election of the Proxy Method vs. Traditional Method

In Part 3, Section A of Form T661, a claimant must elect each taxation year to calculate its SR&ED expenditures using either the Proxy Method (Line 160) or the Traditional Method (Line 162). Pursuant to clauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) and (B) of the ITA, this election is made on a year-by-year basis; however, once Form T661 is filed for a taxation year, the choice between the proxy and traditional methods is strictly irrevocable for that taxation year.

body.text: Worked Comparison: Proxy vs. Traditional Method (2025/2026 Rules)

To illustrate the financial divergence between the two methods, consider a Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (Lakehead Instruments Inc.) with a December 31, 2025 taxation year-end that incurs $800,000 in directly engaged non-specified employee salaries, $100,000 in materials consumed, $200,000 in arm's length Canadian SR&ED subcontractor payments (80% eligible = $160,000), $150,000 in directly related and incremental factory overhead, and receives $50,000 in provincial R&D tax credits.

Under the Proxy Method, the base qualified expenditures before overhead and assistance equal $800,000 (wages) + $100,000 (materials) + $160,000 (80% of contract) = $1,060,000. The Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is calculated at 55% of the $800,000 directly engaged salary base, adding $440,000. After subtracting the $50,000 provincial assistance, total qualified SR&ED expenditures equal $1,060,000 + $440,000 − $50,000 = $1,450,000, which at the 35% enhanced rate yields a fully refundable federal ITC of $507,500. Conversely, under the Traditional Method, the company claims its actual identified overhead of $150,000 instead of the $440,000 PPA, resulting in total qualified SR&ED expenditures of $1,060,000 + $150,000 − $50,000 = $1,160,000 and a 35% federal ITC of $406,000. In this scenario, electing the proxy method yields $101,500 more in refundable federal tax credits while eliminating the audit burden of substantiating individual overhead invoices.
3.2 Salaries and Wages: Scope, Inclusions, and Exclusions

Under subsection 248(1) of the ITA, "salary or wages" means the income of a taxpayer from an office or employment as computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I of the Act. To qualify for SR&ED, the remuneration must be incurred and paid (in the year or within 180 days of year-end) for SR&ED carried on in Canada (Lines 300 and 305 of Form T661) or permissible foreign SR&ED (Lines 307 and 309).

Whether an employee is "directly engaged" in SR&ED (the threshold required under the proxy method) depends strictly on the hands-on tasks performed rather than the employee's job title. Directly engaged tasks include performing experiments and analysis, preparing equipment and materials for trials, directly supervising hands-on SR&ED work, and preparing technical documentation of the SR&ED work. Under the traditional method, salaries and wages of employees who directly undertake, supervise, or support SR&ED (other than directly engaged hands-on work), as well as clerical and administrative staff providing direct services to SR&ED employees, are claimed as overhead and other expenditures on Line 360 rather than as direct wages.

For regular (non-specified) employees, allowable SR&ED salary or wages include regular salaries, hourly wages, vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, regular sick leave pay, pay in lieu of termination notice, tips or gratuities, honorariums, director's or management fees, commissions, inducements, non-competition payments, bonuses, remuneration based on profits, and taxable benefits under Section 6 of the ITA (such as automobile benefits, housing/meals, group term life insurance, or employer savings plan contributions, provided a cash outlay is incurred or a reasonable non-cash cost estimate excluding GST/HST/PST is used and not deducted elsewhere). Conversely, SR&ED salary or wages strictly exclude the employer's share of payroll-related benefits (such as employer CPP, EI, or WCB contributions, which can only be claimed as Line 360 overhead under the traditional method), extended vacation or extended sick leave (since the employee is not performing SR&ED), stock option benefits (deemed not to be an SR&ED expenditure), retiring allowances (which may partially qualify as Line 360 overhead under the traditional method if incremental and allocated based on career SR&ED service), and shareholder dividends (which do not constitute employment income).
3.3 Specified Employees: Statutory Caps and Proxy Salary Base Restrictions

The Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations impose two distinct tiers of statutory restrictions on remuneration paid to "specified employees"—shareholder-employees or employees who do not deal at arm's length with the claimant corporation as defined in subsection 248(1) of the ITA.
Tier 1: Allowable SR&ED Salary or Wages Cap (Section 37 & Part 3 of Form T661)

When calculating allowable SR&ED salary or wages in Part 3 of Form T661 (Lines 305 and 309), subsection 37(9) of the ITA strictly prohibits including any bonus or remuneration based on profits paid to a specified employee. Furthermore, under subsection 37(9.1) of the ITA, the maximum amount of regular SR&ED salary or wages that may be claimed for a specified employee in a taxation year is capped by the formula 5 × YMPE × (B ÷ 365), where YMPE is the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, and B is the number of days in the taxation year that the individual was a specified employee. Under subsections 37(9.2) to 37(9.5) of the ITA, if a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations, no SR&ED salary or wages may be claimed by any of those corporations unless they file an agreement on prescribed Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)), accompanied by a certified copy of a directors' resolution (or sole shareholder confirmation), allocating the single 5× YMPE limit across the associated group.
Tier 2: Proxy Method Salary Base Cap (Regulation 2900(7) & Part 5 of Form T661)

When a claimant elects the Proxy Method, calculating the salary base (Line 818 of Form T661) upon which the 55% PPA is computed requires first excluding all taxable benefits, bonuses, profit-based remuneration, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year (Line 310) for all employees under Regulation 2900(9) (reported on Line 812). Next, for each specified employee (calculated in Boxes 850 to 860 of Form T661), subsections 2900(7) and 2900(8) of the Income Tax Regulations restrict the amount includable in the proxy salary base to the lesser of two statutory limits:

items: 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages for the taxation year (including both SR&ED and non-SR&ED employment duties in Box 852, but excluding bonuses, profit-based remuneration, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid amounts), enforced on Form T661 by capping the percentage of time spent directly engaged in SR&ED in Box 854 at a maximum of 75%; or

2.5 × YMPE × (B ÷ 365) (reported in Box 858), where YMPE is the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings for the calendar year in which the tax year ends and B is the number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual. As clarified in Section 4.1 of the CRA's Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy, there is no proration under this second limit for the portion of the year during which the employee was not a specified employee. Furthermore, under Regulation 2900(5) and 2900(6), the total PPA calculated at 55% of the salary base is subject to an overall cap where total business deductions (excluding CCA, the SR&ED deduction on Schedule 1 Line 411, building rent, and interest) are less than the combined proxy and direct expenses.

3.4 Permissible Foreign Salary or Wages (The 10% Rule)

While SR&ED expenditures must generally be incurred for work carried on physically within Canada (including Canada's Exclusive Economic Zone, airspace, seabed, and subsoil under subsection 37(1.3)), subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) of the ITA permit a claimant to include a limited amount of "permissible salary or wages" for SR&ED work performed outside Canada (reported on Lines 307 and 309 of Form T661). To qualify, the work outside Canada must be performed directly by an employee of the claimant (work performed outside Canada by a contractor is strictly ineligible), the employee must be a resident of Canada at the time the expense was incurred, and the foreign SR&ED work must be undertaken solely in support of Canadian SR&ED carried on by the taxpayer. Under subsection 37(1.5), the total deductible outside-Canada salary or wages claimed in the taxation year is limited to the lesser of the actual qualifying foreign SR&ED wages incurred or 10% of the total SR&ED salary or wages paid to employees for SR&ED carried on directly in Canada (meaning the combined total of Lines 307 and 309 cannot exceed 10% of Line 306 on Form T661).
3.5 The 180-Day Unpaid Amounts Rule (Wages vs. Non-Wage Expenditures)

The Income Tax Act enforces strict cash-settlement rules for accrued expenses at year-end, operating through two separate statutory provisions depending on whether the expense is employee remuneration or a non-wage current expenditure.

For unpaid salary or wages under subsection 78(4) of the ITA, any remuneration incurred in a taxation year that remains unpaid on the 180th day after the end of that taxation year is deemed not to have been incurred in that tax year; instead, it is deemed to be incurred in the subsequent taxation year in which it is actually paid (payment on the 180th day satisfies the rule). On Form T661, accrued wages unpaid after 180 days must be identified on Line 315 (and excluded from the current year's claim), and when paid in a future year, they are claimed on Line 310. However, even when paid and claimed on Line 310 in a subsequent year, prior-year unpaid wages (along with reasonable vacation/holiday pay and salary deferral arrangements deemed paid) are permanently excluded from the proxy salary base under Regulation 2900(9), meaning they never generate the 55% PPA.

For unpaid non-wage current expenditures (such as materials, arm's length contracts, third-party payments, or traditional overhead), subsection 127(26) of the ITA stipulates that an amount incurred in a taxation year but not paid within 180 days of the end of that taxation year is deemed not to have been incurred in that year for Section 127 ITC purposes and must be deducted from qualified expenditures on Line 520 of Form T661. When the unpaid expenditure is subsequently paid in a future taxation year, it is added back to qualified expenditures on Line 500. Crucially, per the CRA's Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for Investment Tax Credit Purposes Policy, an unpaid amount must be formally identified on Form T661 within the 18-month reporting deadline for the taxation year in which it was originally incurred; if it is not identified by that deadline, it can never be included in qualified expenditures in any future year when paid. Furthermore, if the unpaid expenditure is an arm's length SR&ED contract (for example, $100,000 incurred in 2024 and paid in September 2025), 20% ($20,000) is first deducted on Line 529, the remaining 80% ($80,000) is deducted as unpaid on Line 520 in 2024, and when paid in 2025, only 80% ($80,000) is added to qualified expenditures on Line 500.
3.6 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed

Under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) of the ITA (proxy method) and paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the Income Tax Regulations (traditional method), a claimant may include the cost of materials that are either consumed (Line 320) or transformed (Line 325) in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Per the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy, materials must be physical, tangible substances or objects (existing in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) purchased from Canadian or foreign suppliers and used directly as the body or object upon which SR&ED is carried out in Canada. The claimable cost includes the invoice price, customs and excise duties, transportation, and third-party processing service costs (such as the cost of galvanizing metal parts prior to destructive testing). Costs may only be claimed in the taxation year in which the materials are actually consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED, not when they are merely purchased for inventory.

Materials consumed (Line 320) are materials destroyed or rendered virtually valueless during the SR&ED testing. Under the proxy method, broken or used lab supplies, cleaning supplies, general utilities (water, electricity, oil, natural gas), CDs/DVDs, and used lubricants do not qualify as materials consumed because they are overhead items covered by the PPA, whereas under the traditional method they may be claimed on Line 360 if directly related and incremental (and energy used directly in the prosecution of SR&ED may qualify under specific conditions). Materials transformed (Line 325) are materials incorporated or transformed into experimental production, pilot plants, or prototypes during SR&ED that retain commercial value at the end of testing (excluding any excess production beyond what is required for SR&ED). While materials transformed are 100% deductible and eligible for ITCs in the year of transformation, they are subject to the 20-year ITC Recapture regime under subsections 127(27) to 127(36) if the resulting property (such as experimental fabric woven from claimed yarn) is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use.
3.7 Overhead and Other Expenditures Under the Traditional Method

Claimants electing the Traditional Method on Line 162 may claim actual overhead and other current expenditures on Line 360 of Form T661, governed by paragraph 2900(2)(c) and subsection 2900(3) of the Income Tax Regulations. Per the CRA's SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy, an indirect expense qualifies on Line 360 only if it satisfies two cumulative tests. First, under the Directly Related Test, the expenditure must connect directly—with no intervening step or intermediary—to the SR&ED work, the SR&ED staff, or the machinery and equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED. Second, under the Incremental Test, the expenditure must be one that would not have been incurred had the SR&ED prosecution not occurred.

Applying these two tests yields specific audit rules for common corporate expenses under the traditional method. Qualifying traditional overheads include the employer's share of related benefits and retiring allowances for hands-on SR&ED staff (for example, if an employee spent 60% of their career on SR&ED, 60% of a $210,000 incremental retiring allowance, or $126,000, is directly attributable); salaries and wages of clerical and administrative staff providing direct services (accounting, HR, purchasing) to SR&ED employees (though related benefits, retiring allowances, training, and travel for such administrative staff fail the direct linkage test and are disallowed); travel and lodging expenses within Canada for hands-on SR&ED staff to conduct testing at a customer location; training costs in Canada for hands-on SR&ED staff; properly allocated incremental utilities; technical periodical subscriptions; waste and scrap disposal costs incurred during SR&ED prosecution (waste disposal after the project ends fails the test); moving expenses to relocate SR&ED employees or selected candidates within Canada and related housing-loss taxable benefits; and fees paid to volunteers participating in clinical studies.

Conversely, recruitment expenses incurred prior to hiring—specifically headhunter fees, job advertising, candidate interview travel, and immigration/work permit costs—are deductible only as regular business expenses and do not qualify for SR&ED. Regular monthly telephone, cellular, and internet fees also fail the incremental test (only identifiable incremental long-distance charges for SR&ED qualify). Finally, paragraph 2902(a) of the Income Tax Regulations designates specific items as prescribed expenditures that are statutorily barred from earning ITCs even if they are directly related and incremental to SR&ED: fees paid to consultants or advisors for preparing SR&ED claims, costs to attend conventions or conferences, interest and financing expenses under paragraphs 20(1)(c) to (g) of the ITA, dues or membership fees in scientific or technical societies, entertainment, advertising, or selling expenses, fines or penalties, and general legal or accounting fees.
4. Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment, and Lease Costs
4.1 Reinstatement of Capital Expenditure Eligibility (Bill C-15)

Between January 1, 2014, and December 15, 2024, capital expenditures (depreciable property) and equipment lease costs were completely excluded from both the Section 37 deduction pool and Section 127 qualified expenditures. Enacted on March 26, 2026, Bill C-15 amended subsection 37(1) of the ITA by reintroducing paragraph 37(1)(b) and repealing the exclusionary rules in paragraph 37(8)(d) and subsections 37(14) and 37(15).

Under the restored rules—codified in the CRA's updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026), and SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (May 22, 2026)—capital property acquired after December 15, 2024 (i.e., on or after December 16, 2024), and equipment lease costs that first become payable on or after December 16, 2024, once again qualify for SR&ED deductions and ITCs. This legislative restoration is particularly impactful for capital-intensive Canadian industries, including artificial intelligence and machine learning (where GPU clusters and compute infrastructure now qualify for the first time since 2014), hardware engineering, advanced manufacturing, clean technology, and biotechnology.
4.2 Depreciable Property Meeting the "All or Substantially All" (ASA ≥90%) Test

Under paragraph 37(1)(b) and subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III) (traditional method) and 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(III) (proxy method) of the ITA, a claimant may include 100% of the capital cost of depreciable property (including purchase price, installation costs, customs and excise duties, transportation, and other acquisition costs) on Line 390 of Form T661—and must list the names and SR&ED operating time percentages of the 10 most expensive SR&ED properties on Lines 262 and 263 of Form T661—if the property satisfies all statutory criteria.

First, the asset (which may be new or used depreciable property, subject to prescribed rules for used or non-arm's length property under subsection 127(11.6)) must be acquired after December 15, 2024, and under the available-for-use rule in subsection 37(1.2) of the ITA, the expenditure is deemed not to have been made until the taxation year in which the property becomes available for use. Second, at the time of acquisition, the claimant must intend either that the property will be used during all or substantially all (ASA, defined as 90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life in the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada, or that all or substantially all (90% or more) of its value will be consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada.

Under subsection 37(6) of the ITA, any amount deducted under subsection 37(1) in respect of an SR&ED capital expenditure is deemed to be Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) allowed to the taxpayer under paragraph 20(1)(a), and the SR&ED property is deemed to be of a separate prescribed class. Consequently, capital expenditures claimed on Line 390 of Form T661 must not be included on Schedule T2SCH8 (Capital Cost Allowance), preventing double deductions. If a capital expenditure is not claimed on Form T661 by the 18-month reporting deadline, it can only be depreciated under regular CCA rules on Schedule 8. Disposing of claimed SR&ED capital property may trigger both CCA recapture under subsection 13(1) (reported on Line 440 of Form T661) and SR&ED ITC recapture under subsection 127(27).

Non-depreciable capital assets (such as land, inventory, or goodwill) never qualify as SR&ED capital expenditures. Moreover, under paragraph 37(8)(e) of the ITA, capital expenditures made to acquire a building or a leasehold interest in a building are strictly excluded from SR&ED (other than a prescribed special-purpose building under Regulation 2903, or specific third-party payments). For capital assets that do not qualify for SR&ED, Bill C-15 also enacted parallel immediate CCA expensing on Schedule 8 for qualifying property acquired on or after April 16, 2024, and available for use before January 1, 2027, in Class 44 (patents or rights to use patented information), Class 46 (data network infrastructure equipment and related systems software), and Class 50 (general-purpose electronic data-processing equipment and systems software), alongside a reinstated Accelerated Investment Incentive (AII) for eligible property acquired after 2024 and available for use before 2030.
4.3 Shared-Use Equipment (SUE): First-Term and Second-Term Mechanics

When depreciable property is used in an environment combining SR&ED and commercial production and does not satisfy the ≥90% ASA test, it may qualify as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) under subsection 127(9) of the ITA (claimed on Line 504, Boxes 782 and 792 of Form T661). The SUE calculation is identical under both the Traditional Method and the Proxy Method.

To qualify as First-Term SUE, the property must be: (1) depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024; (2) new property (never used, acquired for use, or rented for any purpose before acquisition); (3) not eligible as ≥90% ASA SR&ED capital property; (4) not General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF) (office desks, chairs, lamps, filing cabinets, photocopiers, fax machines, telephones, and calculators are excluded as GPOEF, whereas computers, hardware, software, and ancillary equipment are not GPOEF); (5) not Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under Regulation 2900(11); and (6) actually used primarily (more than 50%) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada during the First Period. The First Period begins when the property becomes available for use and ends at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months after that time. If actual SR&ED operating time in the First Period exceeds 50%, 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost of the equipment (calculated without borrowing costs under Section 21 or deemed capital cost rules under subsections 13(7.1) and 13(7.4), and adjusted for non-arm's length costs under subsection 127(11.6)) is included as a qualified expenditure on Line 504.

To qualify as Second-Term SUE, the equipment must have qualified as First-Term SUE and must be actually used primarily (more than 50%) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada cumulatively during the Second Period—which begins when the property becomes available for use and ends at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after that time. If satisfied, an additional 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost is claimed as a qualified expenditure on Line 504 in that second taxation year. Unlike ≥90% ASA capital property, the capital cost of SUE is not part of the Section 37 deductible SR&ED expenditure pool; instead, the claimant depreciates the cost under regular CCA rules on Schedule T2SCH8, and any ITC earned and applied or refunded for SUE reduces the Undepreciated Capital Cost (UCC) of the CCA class in the subsequent year.

Auditors strictly enforce the Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) exclusion under subsection 2900(11) of the Income Tax Regulations. Property is classified as PDP—and completely barred from SUE and ITC eligibility—if, at the time of acquisition, the claimant intended to use it in SR&ED during the assembly, construction, or commissioning of a facility, plant, or line for commercial manufacturing, processing, or other commercial purposes, and intended that over its expected useful life it would be used primarily (>50%) for non-SR&ED commercial purposes (or have its value consumed primarily in non-SR&ED activities). Because PDP status is determined by intended use at acquisition over the asset's useful life, equipment incorporated into a commercial production line remains excluded as PDP even if unforeseen commissioning trials cause actual SR&ED usage during the first 12 to 24 months to exceed 50%.
4.4 Equipment Lease Costs, Software Licences, Cloud Computing, and Bandwidth

For lease costs that first become payable after December 15, 2024, the tax treatment of leased equipment depends on the claimant's overhead method election and the percentage of operating time (calculated across the entire 12-month taxation year, or the post-December 15, 2024 portion of a transition year) that the equipment is used for SR&ED in Canada.

Under the Proxy Method, if leased equipment (excluding GPOEF) is used 90% or more (ASA) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada, 100% of the lease cost can be claimed (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I)). If the leased equipment (excluding GPOEF) is used primarily (>50% to <90%) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada, 50% of the lease cost can be claimed (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI)). If the equipment is used 50% or less of its operating time for SR&ED, no lease cost can be claimed under the proxy method.

Under the Traditional Method, if leased equipment (including GPOEF) is used 90% or more (ASA) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada, 100% of the lease cost can be claimed as a lease expenditure (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)). If the leased equipment is used less than 90% of its operating time for SR&ED, a proportional amount of the lease cost based on actual SR&ED operating time can be claimed on Line 360 as overhead and other expenditures, provided the expense is directly related and incremental under Regulation 2900(2)(c).

Outlays or rent for the use of, or right to use, a building are strictly excluded under both methods (paragraph 37(8)(e)), unless the building is a Finance-approved prescribed special-purpose building. Where a single lease agreement covers both a building and equipment, the claimant must make a reasonable allocation between excluded building rent and eligible equipment lease costs. Lease costs for land are excluded under the proxy method (as land is not a premise, facility, or equipment and is covered by the PPA), but are allowable as overhead on Line 360 under the traditional method if ASA or directly attributable and incremental to SR&ED in Canada.

Per Section 4.1 and Section 4.2 of the SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy and the SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy, whether a contract is a lease or a sale is determined by the formal legal relationship established by the agreement (Shell Canada Limited v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5669), and software or software licences (including systems software and rights/licences to use software) may qualify either as an SR&ED capital expenditure or as a current lease expenditure depending on the legal facts of the agreement. Furthermore, under Section 4.3.1 of the SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy—applying the Tax Court of Canada precedent in Data Kinetics Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1877, where leasing a dedicated telephone line and remote mainframe was held to be a lease of sophisticated optoelectronic and compute equipment rather than GPOEF—costs incurred after December 15, 2024, for dedicated bandwidth qualify as an allowable lease of equipment under the proxy method, provided the bandwidth is dedicated to SR&ED and is not general office internet (GPOEF).
5. Subcontractors, Non-Arm's Length Transactions, and Third-Party Payments
5.1 Arm's Length SR&ED Contracts (The 80% Inclusion Rule)

A claimant may contract out eligible SR&ED work (basic research, applied research, experimental development, or paragraph (d) support work) to an arm's length contractor, claimed on Line 340 of Form T661 under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) of the ITA. To qualify, the contractor must perform the SR&ED work in Canada on behalf of the claimant (any offshore portion of a contract does not qualify). Per the CRA's Contract Expenditures for SR&ED Performed on Behalf of a Claimant Policy, work is performed "on behalf of" the payer when the payer controls the SR&ED work and retains exclusive rights to the results. Furthermore, following the repeal of former subsections 37(14) and 37(15) by Bill C-15, contract expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024, are no longer reduced by the performer's capital or equipment lease costs.

Under subsection 127(9) of the ITA, an arm's length contract expenditure earns an ITC only if it is paid or payable to a "taxable supplier". Amounts paid or payable to a person or partnership that is not a taxable supplier must be deducted from qualified expenditures on Line 528 of Form T661. While 100% of an eligible arm's length contract expenditure enters the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool (Line 400), subsection 127(9) limits the amount included in qualified expenditures for Section 127 ITC purposes to 80% of the eligible contract expenditure (enforced by deducting 20% of Line 340 on Line 529 of Form T661). For the contractor (performer), the amount received or receivable from the payer constitutes a "contract payment" under subsection 127(9), which reduces the performer's own qualified expenditures under subsection 127(18) (reported on Line 517), ensuring that only the payer—and not the performer—claims the ITC.
5.2 Non-Arm's Length (NAL) Contracts and Form T1146 Transfers

When a claimant enters into an SR&ED contract with a person or partnership with whom it does not deal at arm's length (a non-arm's length or NAL performer under Section 251 of the ITA), special statutory rules apply under subsections 37(13), 127(9), 127(11.6), and 127(13). Under subsection 37(13) of the ITA, work performed by a NAL performer for the payer that would be SR&ED if performed directly by the payer (such as linked support work) is deemed to be SR&ED of the performer.

Under paragraph (f) of the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9) of the ITA, the payer's expenditure on a NAL SR&ED contract (reported on Line 345 of Form T661) is an allowable Section 37 expenditure, but is excluded from the payer's qualified SR&ED expenditures and earns no ITC in the hands of the payer. Simultaneously, the amount received or receivable by the NAL performer is not considered a "contract payment", enabling the NAL performer to claim its own underlying SR&ED expenditures and qualified expenditures for ITC purposes. Alternatively, under subsection 127(13) of the ITA, the NAL performer and the NAL payer may file a joint agreement on prescribed Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length, updated May 15, 2026) to transfer all or a portion of the performer's qualified SR&ED expenditures (including the performer's PPA, capped at the contract amount) to the payer. The performer reports the transferred amount on Line 540, and the payer adds it on Line 508 of Form T661. Note that partnerships cannot transfer or receive qualified expenditures on Form T1146 because a partnership is not a "person" for purposes of subsection 127(13). Additionally, when a claimant purchases goods, services, or capital property (other than an SR&ED contract) from a NAL supplier, subsection 127(11.6) limits the qualified expenditure to the actual cost to the NAL supplier (reported on Lines 541–544 of Form T661).
5.3 Third-Party Payments (Universities, Research Institutes, and Consortia)

Distinct from an SR&ED contract performed on behalf of a claimant, a third-party payment (claimed on Line 370 of Form T661 and reported on prescribed Form T1263, Third-Party Payments for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)) is a payment made to certain approved or tax-exempt entities to be used for SR&ED carried on in Canada. Under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1), (ii), and (iii) of the ITA and the CRA's Third-Party Payments Policy, eligible recipients include: (1) a corporation resident in Canada (an "A entity" under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.1)); (2) an approved association that undertakes SR&ED, an approved university, college, research institute, or similar institution, a tax-exempt non-profit SR&ED corporation resident in Canada under paragraph 149(1)(j), or an approved organization funding such entities ("B to E entities" under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(ii)); or (3) for corporate claimants, a paragraph 149(1)(j) non-profit SR&ED corporation conducting basic or applied research in Canada whose primary purpose is use by the claimant in conjunction with its own SR&ED (subparagraph 37(1)(a)(iii)).

To qualify, the payment must be for SR&ED carried on in Canada, the SR&ED must be related to a business of the claimant, and the claimant must be entitled to exploit the results of that SR&ED in their business as a direct result of the payment (if a payment is invested in an endowment and only investment income funds SR&ED, only the principal portion applied to SR&ED as specified in the written agreement qualifies). Like arm's length contracts, eligible third-party payments on Line 370 are 100% deductible under Section 37, but are 80% eligible (subject to a 20% reduction on Line 529) when computing qualified expenditures for the Section 127 ITC.
6. Federal Investment Tax Credit Rates, Thresholds, Refundability, and Recapture
6.1 Basic (15%) vs. Enhanced (35%) Federal ITC Rates

Under subsection 127(9) of the ITA (definition of "specified percentage") and subsection 127(10.1), the federal SR&ED program provides two volume-based Investment Tax Credit rates. The Basic ITC Rate of 15% applies to all qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred by corporations that are neither CCPCs nor ECPCs, qualified expenditures of CCPCs and ECPCs that exceed their annual expenditure limit, and qualified expenditures of individuals (sole proprietorships), trusts, and partnerships. The Enhanced ITC Rate of 35% (comprising the 15% basic rate plus a 20% enhancement) applies to qualified SR&ED expenditures up to the annual Expenditure Limit ($6,000,000 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024; $3,000,000 for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024) incurred by a corporation that is throughout the taxation year either a Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC) or an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC).
6.2 Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) Under Bill C-15

Prior to Bill C-15, a Canadian technology or energy company that went public immediately lost its CCPC status and forfeited access to the 35% refundable ITC. Effective for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, subsection 127(9) of the ITA defines an "eligible Canadian public corporation" (ECPC) as either an "eligible subsidiary" or a corporation that throughout the taxation year meets four statutory conditions:

items: It is resident in Canada (subparagraph (a)(i));

It is a public corporation as defined in subsection 89(1) of the ITA, or would be a public corporation if the words "designated stock exchange in Canada" were read as "designated stock exchange" (capturing Canadian-resident corporations listed on designated foreign stock exchanges) (subparagraph (a)(ii));
It is not controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons (subparagraph (a)(iii)); and

It would not, if each share of its capital stock owned by a non-resident person were owned by a particular person, be controlled by that particular person (adapting the hypothetical single non-resident shareholder aggregation test to publicly traded corporations) (subparagraph (a)(iv)).

body.text: 6.3 The $6 Million Expenditure Limit and Phase-Out Formulas

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the maximum annual expenditure limit for both stand-alone/associated CCPCs and stand-alone/consolidated-group ECPCs is $6,000,000 (reduced proportionally for short taxation years or multiple taxation years in a calendar year). Associated CCPCs must file an agreement on Schedule T2SCH49 (updated May 29, 2026) under subsection 127(10.3) to allocate the single shared $6,000,000 expenditure limit among group members, and consolidated ECPC groups must similarly allocate a single shared expenditure limit.

Under the modernized rules enacted by Bill C-15 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is phased out between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000 using one of two statutory methods. Under the Taxable Capital Method (Default for CCPCs – Subsection 127(10.2)), the $6,000,000 expenditure limit begins to decrease when the CCPC's (and its associated corporations') taxable capital employed in Canada (under sections 181.2 or 181.3 of the ITA) for the immediately preceding taxation year exceeds $15,000,000, and becomes nil at $75,000,000 (replacing the pre-December 16, 2024 phase-out range of $10,000,000 to $50,000,000).

Under the Gross Revenue Phase-Out Method (Mandatory for ECPCs under Subsections 127(10.6)–(10.64); Elective for CCPCs under Subsections 127(10.31)–(10.32)), the $6,000,000 expenditure limit for an ECPC (or consolidated ECPC group) is progressively reduced when its average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years (or over the actual one or two preceding fiscal years if fewer than three exist) is between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000, becoming nil at $75,000,000. Crucially, under subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32) of the ITA, a CCPC or associated CCPC group may elect on the prescribed form to have its expenditure limit determined using this three-year average gross revenue phase-out ($15M to $75M) instead of the subsection 127(10.2) taxable capital phase-out. Where a CCPC makes this election for a taxation year, the taxable capital phase-out under subsection 127(10.2) does not apply for that year.
6.4 Comprehensive Refundability Matrix (Section 127.1)

Whether an earned SR&ED ITC is refunded in cash (after offsetting Part I tax payable) or remains non-refundable depends on the claimant's classification under Section 127.1 of the ITA and whether the expenditure is of a current or capital nature.

A "Qualifying Corporation" under subsection 127.1(2) is a CCPC throughout the taxation year whose taxable income (combined with associated corporations) for the preceding taxation year did not exceed its Qualifying Income Limit. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the Qualifying Income Limit formula is $500,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000], where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital is $15,000,000 or less, or the lesser of $60,000,000 and the excess of prior-year taxable capital over $15,000,000 (replacing the pre-December 16, 2024 formula of $500,000 × [($40,000,000 − A) ÷ $40,000,000] where A was the excess over $10,000,000). A Qualifying Corporation (other than an excluded corporation) receives a 100% refund on its 35% ITC earned on current expenditures and PPA up to the expenditure limit, a 40% refund on its 35% ITC earned on capital expenditures up to the expenditure limit, and a 40% refund on its 15% basic ITC earned on current and capital expenditures above the expenditure limit.

Under subsection 127.1(2.01), a CCPC that is neither a Qualifying Corporation nor an Excluded Corporation (for example, a CCPC whose prior-year taxable income exceeded $500,000 but whose expenditure limit has not phased out) still receives a 100% refund on its 35% ITC for current expenditures and PPA up to the expenditure limit, and a 40% refund on its 35% ITC for capital expenditures up to the expenditure limit, but receives 0% refundability on any 15% ITC earned over the expenditure limit. Similarly, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) receives a 100% refund on its 35% ITC for current expenditures up to the expenditure limit, a 40% refund on its 35% ITC for capital expenditures up to the expenditure limit, and 0% refundability on any 15% ITC earned over the expenditure limit.
