body.text: 6.5 Partnership Allocation Rules and Loss Restrictions

Because a partnership is not a "person" for tax purposes, a partnership cannot claim an SR&ED ITC directly. Instead, the Section 37 expenditure pool is deducted at the partnership level in computing partnership income, and the Section 127 ITC is calculated at the partnership level solely at the basic 15% rate (even if the partners are CCPCs) and allocated to eligible partners. Per the CRA's SR&ED Claims for Partnerships Policy, the SR&ED ITC allocated to partners reduces the partnership's Section 37 deductible expenditure pool in that same fiscal period.

Furthermore, no SR&ED ITC may be allocated to a "specified member" of a partnership (defined as a limited partner or a passive general partner). Unallocated ITCs of specified members must be reallocated to active general partners (non-specified members) based on a reasonable share considering their partnership investment, or an active partner may elect to formally renounce that reallocated ITC using Form T932 (Election by a Member of a Partnership to Renounce Investment Tax Credits Pursuant to Subsection 127(8.4)), which extinguishes the credit so that it does not reduce the partnership's Section 37 pool. Additionally, a partnership loss created or increased by deducting the Section 37 SR&ED pool cannot be claimed by a limited partner; the limited partner's deductible loss is reduced by the lesser of the SR&ED pool deducted or the partnership loss, and the disallowed loss is permanently extinguished (it does not become a limited partnership loss or non-capital loss and does not adjust the limited partner's adjusted cost base). For trusts, only graduated rate estates and communal organizations deemed to be inter vivos trusts may designate an SR&ED ITC to their beneficiaries.
6.6 Carryback, Carryforward, and Loss Restriction Events (Acquisition of Control)

Unused non-refundable SR&ED ITCs may be carried back 3 taxation years or carried forward up to 20 taxation years to reduce federal Part I tax payable in those years. However, if a corporation undergoes a Loss Restriction Event (an acquisition of control), paragraph 37(1)(h) and subsection 37(6.1) restrict the corporation's ability to carry forward its unused Section 37 expenditure pool, and subsections 127(9.1) and 127(9.2) restrict the carryforward of unused pre-acquisition ITCs and the carryback of unused post-acquisition ITCs.
6.7 The 20-Year ITC Recapture Regime (Subsections 127(27) to 127(36))

To ensure that only the net costs of performing SR&ED attract tax incentives, subsections 127(27) to 127(36) of the ITA reverse all or a portion of previously earned SR&ED ITCs by adding a recaptured amount to Part I tax payable (while allowing the recaptured amount to be added back to the Section 37 expenditure pool in the subsequent year under paragraph 37(1)(c.2), reported on Line 453 of Form T661).

Per the CRA's Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, recapture is triggered when all four statutory conditions are met: (1) the claimant acquired a particular property in the current taxation year or in any of the 20 preceding taxation years; (2) the cost of the property was a qualified expenditure; (3) the cost (or a percentage of it) was included in computing the claimant's ITC at the end of a taxation year; and (4) the claimant disposes of or converts to commercial use the particular property (or another property incorporating it). Recapture applies to materials transformed (Line 325), SR&ED capital property (Line 390), Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) (Line 504), and the property portion of SR&ED contracts (including transferred NAL expenditures under subsection 127(13)), whereas salaries/wages, overhead, intellectual property sales, and materials consumed (unless insurance or scrap proceeds exceed 10% of cost) are not subject to recapture. Under subsection 127(32), "cost" for recapture purposes cannot exceed the amount paid to acquire the property from another person and excludes salaries, wages, or overhead imputed to the property. By CRA administrative policy (the de minimis rule), no recapture applies if proceeds from a scrap sale or the fair market value at the time of commercial conversion are less than 10% of the total cost of the property.
7. Government Assistance, Non-Government Assistance, and Direct Funding Interaction
7.1 Statutory Reduction Rules for Assistance and Contract Payments

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) (for the Section 37 pool) and subsections 127(9) and 127(18) (for Section 127 qualified expenditures) of the ITA, a claimant must reduce its SR&ED expenditures on an accrual basis by any government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payments in respect of SR&ED that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing-due date for the taxation year (Lines 429–432 and Lines 513–517 of Form T661).

Government assistance (subsection 127(9)) includes any grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, investment allowance, or other assistance from a government, municipality, Crown corporation, or public authority, excluding the federal SR&ED ITC itself. All provincial and territorial R&D tax credits constitute government assistance that reduces federal SR&ED expenditures. Non-government assistance is any inducement, reimbursement, contribution, or allowance from a private entity that would be included in income under paragraph 12(1)(x).

Per the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, assistance reductions are applied strictly on a project-by-project basis. Assistance for one project cannot reduce the expenditures of an unrelated project; if project assistance exceeds project costs, that project's qualified expenditures are reduced to nil (with excess assistance included in income under paragraph 12(1)(x) and carried forward to reduce future qualified expenditures on that project under subsection 127(19)). Non-arm's length parties working on the same project can allocate assistance among themselves using prescribed Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length, updated May 15, 2026) under subsection 127(20).

When a claimant elects the Proxy Method, 100% of a provincial R&D tax credit (including the portion earned on the federal 55% PPA) reduces federal qualified expenditures on Lines 513–514 under subsection 127(18). However, because the PPA is not included in the Section 37 deduction pool, the portion of the provincial tax credit relating to the PPA does not reduce the Section 37 pool on Line 429; instead, that PPA-related provincial credit portion must be included directly in income in the year received under paragraph 12(1)(x). Similarly, in Quebec, any portion of a provincial R&D credit earned on support salaries or subcontract support salaries that do not qualify under the federal proxy method is included in income under paragraph 12(1)(x) rather than reducing the Section 37 pool. If assistance or contract payments are subsequently repaid, the repayment is added to the Section 37 pool on Line 445 and to qualified expenditures on Line 560 of Form T661 to earn a non-refundable ITC in the year of repayment.
7.2 The Bill C-69 "Excluded Loan" Exemption (Bona Fide Government Loans)

On June 20, 2024, Bill C-69 received Royal Assent, amending subsection 127(9) of the ITA retroactively to January 1, 2020 (for loans made after December 31, 2019), to state that "excluded loans"—bona fide loans with reasonable repayment terms from public authorities—are not considered government assistance. Consequently, unconditional, repayable innovation loans from government bodies do not reduce a claimant's Section 37 pool or Section 127 qualified expenditures. Conversely, forgivable loans or loans where repayment is contingent upon project profits or royalties remain classified as government assistance.
7.3 Interaction with Direct Federal Innovation Grants (NRC IRAP and SIF)

Canadian businesses routinely stack direct federal innovation grants and provincial R&D credits with federal SR&ED tax incentives, subject to the statutory assistance reduction rules and an overarching 75% total government assistance stacking limit.

Canada's premier direct R&D grant for SMEs is the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP), which provides non-repayable financial contributions ranging from $15,000 up to $500,000 per project (covering R&D salaries and contractor costs), Youth Employment Program wage subsidies, and technical advisory services from Industrial Technology Advisors (ITAs) to incorporated, for-profit Canadian SMEs with 500 or fewer employees. Unlike SR&ED (which is claimed retrospectively after the tax year ends), IRAP is a cost-shared grant that must be negotiated and approved upfront before the project starts. For large-scale industrial R&D and decarbonization projects, the federal Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) provides direct contributions. When stacking provincial credits with federal SR&ED, the provincial credit is calculated first and reduces the federal SR&ED qualified expenditure base; for example, in Quebec, stacking the 30% refundable CRIC credit with the 35% refundable federal SR&ED credit delivers an effective combined R&D assistance rate of approximately 54.5%.
8. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes

In addition to the federal SR&ED program, nine Canadian provinces and one territory offer dedicated R&D tax credits (only Prince Edward Island, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut do not offer a provincial/territorial R&D tax credit). All provincial/territorial credits are administered by the CRA through the T2 corporate return except for Quebec (administered by Revenu Québec) and Alberta (administered by the Province of Alberta).
8.1 Quebec: The Landmark 2025 CRIC Overhaul

In its March 2025 budget, Quebec enacted a sweeping overhaul of its provincial R&D tax system, abolishing its legacy R&D credits (including the former R&D wage credit, university/public research centre credit, private partnership pre-competitive research credit, research consortium fees credit, technological adaptation services credit, the industrial design part of the design credit, and the tax holiday for foreign researchers/experts) and replacing them with the unified, 100% refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) (crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation), effective for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025 (legacy credits remain claimable only for taxation years beginning before March 26, 2025).
The CRIC introduces four structural changes for Quebec claimants:

items: Expansion to Pre-Commercialization Activities: While R&D eligibility remains aligned with federal CRA scientific reviews, CRIC also covers pre-commercialization activities carried out in Quebec that continue R&D already performed in Quebec by or for the claimant—specifically regulatory testing, technological validations, certification studies, and product design (improvements in form, function, materials, or aesthetics).

Eligible Expenditures: Covers (a) 100% of employee salaries and wages for eligible R&D and pre-commercialization work in Quebec; (b) 50% of payments to Quebec subcontractors; (c) 50% of payments to eligible Quebec universities, public research centres, or research consortia (reduced from 80% under the prior regime to align with subcontracting); and (d) capital expenditures to acquire depreciable property used in R&D or pre-commercialization in Quebec (excluding land, buildings, or usage rights; cannot be combined with Quebec's C3i credit on the same expense).

The Exclusion Threshold: Before applying the credit rates, the claimant must subtract an annual Exclusion Threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the basic personal amount (BPA) per employee prorated by each employee's time spent on R&D and pre-commercialization (replacing the prior asset-based threshold of $50,000 to $225,000).

30% / 20% Fully Refundable Credit Rates: Eligible Canadian-controlled corporations earn a 30% fully refundable tax credit on up to $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures above the exclusion threshold (regardless of corporate asset size), and a 20% fully refundable tax credit on qualified expenditures exceeding $1,000,000 (as well as 20% for other corporations and individuals), replacing the legacy 14% basic rate. Corporations claim the CRIC with Revenu Québec on Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (accompanied by Form RD-1029.8.EN-T for group expenditure limit allocations and Form RD-1029.8.PR-T for pre-commercialization details).

body.text: 8.2 Ontario: Three-Tier Stackable Credit System
Corporations with a permanent establishment in Ontario can claim three stackable provincial R&D credits under Sections 38 to 45 of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), all administered by the CRA:

items: Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC – Schedule T2SCH566): An 8% refundable tax credit available to CCPCs on up to $3,000,000 of qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures (maximum $240,000 refund). The $3,000,000 limit remains separate from the $6,000,000 federal limit and phases out when prior-year taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000 or prior-year taxable capital is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000.

Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC): A 20% fully refundable tax credit available to corporations contracting eligible research to a qualifying Ontario research institute, subject to a $20,000,000 annual expenditure cap across associated corporations.

Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC – Schedule T2SCH508): A 3.5% non-refundable tax credit available to any corporation with an Ontario permanent establishment on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures (with no expenditure cap), carrying back 3 years and forward 20 years. A corporation may deliver a written waiver of the ORDTC within 6 months of its tax year-end (or on an amended return) to avoid reducing its federal SR&ED pool.

body.text: 8.3 Alberta: Innovation Employment Grant (IEG)

Enacted under Sections 26.95 to 26.99 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act for R&D spending after December 31, 2020, and administered by the Province of Alberta (AT1 Schedule 29 and Form AT4970, filed within 15 months after the corporation's filing-due date), the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) provides a fully refundable payment on up to $4,000,000 in annual Alberta R&D spending: 8% on eligible spending up to the corporation's base spending level (the average qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the previous 2 years), and an enhanced 20% on eligible spending exceeding that two-year base level.
8.4 Saskatchewan: March 2026 Budget Expansion & Patent Box (SCII)

Under Sections 63 to 63.4 of The Income Tax Act, 2000 (Saskatchewan) (Schedule T2SCH403), Saskatchewan provides a 10% Research and Development Tax Credit. In the March 18, 2026 Saskatchewan Budget, the province doubled the annual qualifying expenditure limit on which a CCPC claims a 100% refundable 10% credit from $1,000,000 to $2,000,000 (increasing the maximum annual refundable credit from $100,000 to $200,000) and restored the eligibility of capital expenditures (new machinery, equipment, and related lease/rental costs), expected to apply to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. Non-CCPCs and CCPC expenditures above $2,000,000 earn a 10% non-refundable credit (carrying back 3 years and forward 10 years, or 20 years in some program summaries, and eligible for renunciation), with combined refundable and non-refundable credits capped at $1,000,000 per corporation per year ($10,000,000 in spending).

Additionally, Saskatchewan offers North America's first "patent box" regime—the Saskatchewan Commercial Innovation Incentive (SCII) (open for intake through June 30, 2027)—which reduces the provincial Corporate Income Tax rate from 12% to 6% for 10 consecutive years on taxable income derived from commercializing qualifying intellectual property (patents, plant breeders' rights, trade secrets, and copyrights for computer programs/algorithms) in Saskatchewan, extended to 15 consecutive years if at least 50% of the underlying R&D was performed in Saskatchewan.
8.5 British Columbia, Manitoba, Atlantic Provinces, and Yukon

items: British Columbia (Sections 97 to 103, Income Tax Act (BC) – Form T666): Provides a 10% tax credit (18-month filing deadline), which is 100% refundable for CCPCs and, for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) on expenditures up to the federal expenditure limit, now $6,000,000 ($600,000 max refund; previously $3,000,000 and $300,000), and non-refundable above that limit or for other corporations (carryback 3 years, carryforward 10 years; can be renounced). Bill 2, the Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026 (S.B.C. 2026, c. 5), enacted these changes and removed the credit's former September 1, 2027 expiry date.

Manitoba (Section 7.3, Income Tax Act (Manitoba) – Schedule T2SCH380): Provides a 15% tax credit (filed within 1 year after the filing-due date). For in-house R&D, one-half (7.5%) is refundable and one-half (7.5%) is non-refundable (carryback 3 years, carryforward 20 years; can be renounced up to 1 year after the filing-due date), while R&D performed under contract with a qualifying institute is 100% refundable (15%).

Nova Scotia (T2SCH340, s. 41 ITA (NS)), New Brunswick (T2SCH360, s. 59 NB ITA), and Newfoundland and Labrador (T2SCH301 / T1129, s. 42 ITA (NL)): Each of these three Atlantic provinces provides a 15% fully refundable tax credit with no dollar expenditure cap (in Newfoundland and Labrador, eligible expenditures are not reduced by other government assistance except GST/HST input tax credits).

Yukon (T2SCH442 / T1232, s. 15 ITA (Yukon)): Provides a 15% fully refundable tax credit (filed within 12 months after the filing-due date), plus an additional 5% refundable credit (20% total) on amounts paid or payable to Yukon University.

body.text: 9. Filing Procedures, Pre-Claim Approval, Compliance, and CRA Audit Defence
9.1 Prescribed Forms and 2026 Line-by-Line Updates (Form T661 (26))

To claim federal SR&ED tax incentives, a taxpayer must file prescribed Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim, updated May 15, 2026) together with Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations, updated May 22, 2026) for corporations, or Form T2038(IND) (Investment Tax Credit (Individuals)) for individuals and trusts.

Following Royal Assent of Bill C-15, the CRA released the revised Form T661 (26) on May 15, 2026, structured across ten parts. Part 1 (Lines 010 to 157) captures general claimant and partnership information and the total number of projects claimed (Line 050). Part 2 (Project Information – Sections A, B, and C) must be completed and maintained at the claimant's place of business for every project claimed; however, under the CRA's Top 20 Projects Rule (SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy), a claimant may choose to submit Part 2 upon filing for only the 20 largest projects in dollar value, provided all project costs are reported in Part 6 and complete Part 2 descriptions for all other projects are maintained and provided upon CRA request (failure to provide them upon request results in disallowance of those projects).

Within Part 2, Section A includes new Line 207 (requiring a 5-digit Field of Research (FOR) code from Statistics Canada's CRDC 2020 v2.0) and new Lines 212 and 214 (checkbox and Case Number for Pre-Claim Approval). Section B houses the three core technical narrative fields with strict word limits: Line 242 (scientific or technological uncertainties attempted to be overcome, maximum 350 words), Line 244 (work performed in the tax year to overcome those uncertainties, maximum 700 words), and Line 246 (scientific or technological advancements achieved or attempted, maximum 350 words). Section C identifies key personnel and qualifications (Lines 260/261), project planning evidence checklists (Lines 270–282), and new Lines 262 and 263, requiring the names and SR&ED operating time percentages of the 10 most expensive depreciable properties acquired after December 15, 2024, claimed on Line 390.

Part 3 (Lines 160–470) records the irrevocable method election (Line 160 Proxy vs. Line 162 Traditional), allowable SR&ED expenditures (Lines 300–400, including restored Line 390 capital expenditures), and the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool calculation (Lines 429–470, including Line 440 sale of SR&ED capital assets / CCA recapture). Part 4 (Lines 500–570) calculates total qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes, adding prior paid amounts (Line 500), the PPA (Line 502), restored Shared-Use Equipment on Line 504 (Box 782 capital expenditure amount and Box 792 25% of capital cost), and transferred NAL expenditures (Line 508), and subtracting assistance (Lines 513–517, including Line 514 provincial/territorial assistance), unpaid non-wage amounts (Line 520), non-taxable suppliers (Line 528), the 20% contract/third-party reduction (Line 529), prescribed expenditures (Line 530), and other deductions (Lines 533/535) to arrive at total qualified expenditures on Line 570 (which flows to Schedule T2SCH31, Lines 350/370, or Form T2038(IND), Line 6712). Part 5 (Lines 810–820 & Boxes 850–860) calculates the salary base (Line 818) and the 55% PPA (Line 820). Part 6 (Boxes 750–758) allocates costs by project; Part 7 (Line 605) provides statistical data; Part 8 is the claim checklist; Part 9 captures mandatory claim preparer disclosures; and Part 10 is the authorized officer certification.
9.2 The Statutory 18-Month Reporting Deadline (Zero Ministerial Discretion)

Under subsection 37(11) and paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) of the ITA, a taxpayer must file Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 (or Form T2038(IND)) containing the prescribed information on or before the day that is 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred:

items: Corporations: Because a corporation's T2 return is due within 6 months of its tax year-end under paragraph 150(1)(a), the corporate SR&ED reporting deadline is 18 months after the end of the taxation year (non-profit SR&ED corporations under paragraph 149(1)(j) must file Form T661 within 6 months of year-end and cannot claim an ITC).

Individuals (Sole Proprietors): Because a self-employed individual's T1 filing-due date is June 15, adding 12 months yields a reporting deadline of June 15 of the following calendar year, or 17.5 months after the December 31 taxation year-end.
Trusts: Because a trust's T3 filing-due date under paragraph 150(1)(c) is 90 days after year-end, adding 12 months yields a reporting deadline of up to 15 months after the end of the taxation year.

Partnerships: Form T661 must be filed with the T5013 Partnership Information Return no later than 12 months after the earliest of all filing-due dates for the income tax returns of the members for the taxation year in which the partnership's fiscal period ends.

body.text: The reporting deadline attaches individually to each expenditure. Under subsections 37(11.1) and 37(12) of the ITA, any expenditure not identified on prescribed Form T661 by the reporting deadline is deemed not to be an SR&ED expenditure and cannot be included in the Section 37 pool or earn an ITC. While a claimant may submit an amended Form T661 to add projects or expenditures before the reporting deadline, the Minister of National Revenue has no statutory mechanism or discretion (including under the taxpayer relief provisions of subsection 220(3.1) of the ITA) to extend the 18-month reporting deadline. Under paragraph 230(4)(b) of the ITA, all books, records, and supporting SR&ED evidence must be retained for six years from the end of the last taxation year to which they relate.
9.3 The New Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026)

On April 1, 2026, the CRA launched its optional Pre-Claim Approval process, allowing eligible businesses to obtain an upfront project eligibility determination before beginning work or incurring significant costs:

items: Confirm Eligibility Criteria: The business must be a CCPC, other Canadian corporation, or partnership, have gross business income of less than $25,000,000, and be in good standing with the CRA; the project must not have been included in a previous SR&ED claim and must not involve issues currently under litigation.

Request a Case Number & Submit Form T1322: Before beginning planned work (or shortly after starting), the claimant requests a Case Number and uploads Form T1322 with supporting project planning documents via My Business Account.

Participate in the RTA Evaluation Meeting: The CRA assigns a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA). For existing SR&ED claimants in good standing, the RTA may request a meeting; for all other businesses, a 2- to 5-hour meeting (virtual or facility tour) with the RTA is mandatory to discuss the existing state of knowledge, the scientific or technological uncertainty, the work to be carried out, and the planned hypothesis and experiments.

Receive the 8-Week Written Determination: Within 8 weeks of receiving the complete application, the RTA issues a written Pre-Claim Approval Evaluation Report confirming whether Pre-Claim Approval is granted.

Post-Filing Review Acceleration: If a pre-approved claim is subsequently selected for an Expenditure-Only Review after Form T661 is filed, the CRA generally processes the claim within 90 calendar days (cutting the standard 180-day review period in half), unless the executed project differed materially from the approved plan or included unapproved projects.

body.text: 9.4 CRA Review Procedures, Dispute Resolution, and Penalties

Upon receipt of Form T661, the CRA risk-assesses the claim and either accepts it as filed or selects it for a Financial Review, Technical Review, or Coordinated Review conducted by a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) (reporting to a Research and Technology Manager, RTM) and a Financial Reviewer (FR) (reporting to a Financial Review Manager, FRM).

During the review (conducted via initial phone call, 30-day information request letter, virtual or on-site interviews with technical and financial staff, and review of contemporaneous dated evidence), the RTA prepares an SR&ED Project Eligibility Report. If adjustments are proposed, the claimant receives a Proposal Package and has 30 days to submit written representations. If concerns remain unresolved, the claimant follows the CRA's three-step dispute resolution process: (1) discuss concerns with the RTA and FR; (2) speak with the RTM and FRM; and (3) request an Administrative Review (which verifies that the review complied with SR&ED legislation, policies, and due process, rather than conducting a second technical review). Once a Notice of Assessment or Reassessment is issued (within the normal reassessment period of 3 years for a CCPC and 4 years for other corporations), the claimant has 90 days from the date of the notice to serve a formal Notice of Objection, followed by the right to appeal to the Tax Court of Canada.
Two specific statutory penalty provisions apply to SR&ED filings:

items: Part 9 Claim Preparer Penalty ($1,000 – Subsections 162(5.1) to 162(5.3) of the ITA): Part 9 of Form T661 requires full disclosure of every claim preparer who accepted consideration to prepare or assist in preparing the claim and their billing arrangement. While missing or incomplete Part 9 information does not disallow the SR&ED claim itself, a $1,000 penalty applies, for which the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally (or solidarily) liable. The CRA also uses the identity of the claim preparer as a risk-assessment factor in audit selection.

Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims (Subsection 163(2) of the ITA): Per the CRA's Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025 and October 29, 2025), if the CRA establishes under its subsection 163(3) burden of proof that a false statement or omission was made knowingly or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence (more than a simple oversight or misunderstanding), a penalty applies equal to the greater of $100 or 50% of the total of: (a) the understated Part I tax payable reasonably attributable to the false statement or omission (paragraph 163(2)(a)), plus (b) the refund of the overstated refundable ITC claimed by the claimant (paragraph 163(2)(d)). When the gross negligence penalty applies to an overstated refundable ITC refund, the CRA calculates the 50% penalty on the entire overstated refund regardless of what caused each portion of the overstatement.

body.text: 10. Controlling Jurisprudence and Judicial Precedents

Because CRA administrative guidelines are not binding on the courts, SR&ED eligibility and evidentiary disputes are governed by the jurisprudence of the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA).
10.1 The Foundational Five-Question Test: Northwest Hydraulic, RIS-Christie, and CW Agencies

In Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC), Chief Justice Bowman established the landmark five-criteria test for determining whether work constitutes SR&ED under subsection 248(1) of the ITA: (1) Was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures? (2) Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty? (3) Did the procedure adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses? (4) Did the process result in a technological advancement? and (5) Was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and the results kept as the work progressed?

The Federal Court of Appeal formally adopted and affirmed the Northwest Hydraulic criteria in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087 (FCA) and CW Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393. In RIS-Christie, the FCA held that while taxpayers must adduce reliable evidence proving that scientific testing took place, contemporaneous documentary evidence under Question 5—though highly advantageous—is not strictly mandatory if the taxpayer provides a plausible explanation and reliable corroborating evidence.
10.2 Reaffirmation of the Scientific Method and Expert Witness Rules: Kam-Press and National R&D

In Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88 (aff'g 2019 TCC 246), the taxpayer argued that because the statutory definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) of the ITA makes no literal reference to the "scientific method", Criterion 3 of Northwest Hydraulic should not be applied. The Federal Court of Appeal rejected this argument, holding that the courts' constitutional role is to interpret and elaborate on the meaning of ITA provisions and reaffirming that all five Northwest Hydraulic criteria—including adherence to the scientific method—are mandatory legal requirements.

In National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72 (aff'g 2020 TCC 47), the Federal Court of Appeal affirmed the denial of software development SR&ED claims, establishing three major appellate principles. First, the FCA rejected the taxpayer's claim that the CRA's August 2021 Guidelines on the eligibility of work (which introduced the "Why" and "How" framework without using the phrase "scientific method") removed the requirement to follow the scientific method, confirming that CRA guidance is not binding on the courts and that the "How" requirement still demands underlying experimental rigour consistent with Northwest Hydraulic. Second, the FCA held that attempting to rely on an academic article on appeal to argue for an "engineering method" without introducing expert testimony at trial was an impermissible attempt to establish a fact "through the back door". Third, applying White Burgess Langille Inman v. Abbott and Haliburton Co., 2015 SCC 23, the FCA upheld the exclusion of the taxpayer's proposed expert report because the taxpayer had written the majority of the report, the expert lacked independence and impartiality ("in tone the report was an exercise in advocacy"), and the report usurped the court's function by opining on the legal question of whether the work constituted SR&ED.
10.3 Modern Evidentiary Battles: Canafric (2023), Joel Theatrical (2017), Formadrain (2017), and Tuna Temple (2026)

In Canafric Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 103, the Tax Court of Canada allowed the appeal of a custom frozen food manufacturer whose 2013–2016 SR&ED claims ($343,449 in expenditures and $60,963 in ITCs across disputed projects) had been denied by the CRA. The Tax Court held that (1) technological uncertainty can exist even where publicly available preservation solutions exist, provided they have never been applied in the specific context and constraints of the claimant's product; (2) Canafric did not engage in mere "trial and error" because it systematically analyzed why recipes failed and modified subsequent hypotheses accordingly, and eliminating failed recipes constituted a technological advancement; and (3) impressive, factually grounded oral testimony from the CEO, combined with progressive development records and CRA meeting documentation, satisfied Question 5.

Conversely, in Tuna Temple Inc. v. Canada, 2026 FCA 175 (decided October 21, 2026; aff'g 2025 TCC 183), the Federal Court of Appeal upheld the disallowance of 13 out of 14 SR&ED projects claimed for the 2005–2009 taxation years. Even though the Tax Court found the company's witness credible regarding the projects' structure and intentions to break new ground—and the Crown called no competing witness of its own—the Tax Court found that across the 13 projects there was no hypothesis, the work used existing technology and trial-and-error processes, records were inadequate, and no gap in industry knowledge was established. Dismissing the appeal with costs, the Federal Court of Appeal held that witness credibility alone cannot substitute for objective evidence meeting the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria or refuting the Minister's factual assumptions, and confirmed that the Crown is not required to call a competing witness when the taxpayer's own documents and cross-examination fail to establish a prima facie case.

Rounding out the jurisprudence, Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6 and Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 FCA 355 (aff'g 2011 TCC 261) confirm that where a claimant's staff lack formal engineering training or fail to prove that a problem could not be resolved by routine engineering known to competent professionals, internal difficulty does not establish objective technological uncertainty. Formadrain Inc. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 42 underscores the importance of contemporaneous time and technical documentation in defending SR&ED claims, while Lehigh Hanson Materials Limited v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 205 and 116736 Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 1998 TCC address the strict statutory reporting deadline provisions of subsection 37(11) of the ITA.

Dedicated telecommunications bandwidth and remote mainframe access constitute an allowable lease of equipment (rather than GPOEF overhead) under the proxy method.
Affirms Northwest Hydraulic; clarifies that contemporaneous documentation is the strongest evidence of repeatable testing, though reliable alternative evidence can be considered.
Codifies the succinct five-question formulation of the Northwest Hydraulic criteria at the appellate level.
Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 FCA 355 (aff'g 2011 TCC 261)
Strict burden of proof on the taxpayer to differentiate systematic experimental development from routine shop-floor trial-and-error engineering.
Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6
A gap in a claimant's own internal knowledge or lack of trained engineering staff does not establish an objective technological uncertainty beyond standard engineering practice.
Emphasizes the necessity of credible contemporaneous records to substantiate SR&ED claims and defend against CRA disallowances.
Lehigh Hanson Materials Limited v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 205
Examines the strict statutory reporting deadline mechanics under subsection 37(11) of the ITA.
Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88
Rejects the argument that the "scientific method" is absent from the statute; confirms all five Northwest Hydraulic criteria are binding law.
National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72 (aff'g 2020 TCC 47)
Confirms CRA's 2021 "Why/How" guidelines do not alter the Northwest Hydraulic test; excludes taxpayer-drafted, non-independent expert witness reports under White Burgess.
Technological uncertainty exists when known elements are combined under novel constraints; credible, detailed oral testimony plus progressive records can satisfy Question 5.
Tuna Temple Inc. v. Canada, 2026 FCA 175 (aff'g 2025 TCC 183)
A credible taxpayer witness alone does not demolish the Minister's SR&ED assumptions without objective proof of systematic investigation across each project; Crown need not call a witness.
